question: What product capabilities appear to be most important to prospects?

resolution.read_instruction: Extract every product capability, feature, integration or connector the prospect asks about, requests, praises, or flags as a requirement, concern or deal-breaker, including the prospect's own words on why it matters and any stated priority or urgency.
assumptions: Question concerns prospect calls only (new business), since prospects are the audience named.
Interpreted 'product capabilities' broadly to include features, integrations, security and compliance needs.
Importance is inferred from how often and how emphatically each capability is raised, so the reader should capture stated priority signals.

findings.speaker: Rachel Morgan
findings.quote: we're not looking for another dashboard. We've got dashboards. We need something that actually moves work along and makes it visible who owns what.
findings.context: Prospect's top priority is a workflow layer that moves work along and makes ownership visible, not another dashboard. — Rachel states the core need; explicitly rejects dashboards.

findings.speaker: Rachel Morgan
findings.quote: We're much worse at answering why it was late, or which dependency failed, or whether the same thing happened fifteen times last month.
findings.context: Operational telemetry and visibility into why a process failed is a key gap; prospect wants to know which dependency failed and how often issues recur. — Pain is about root cause and recurrence, not just outcome lateness.

findings.speaker: Rachel Morgan
findings.quote: The happy path is not the hard part. Anyone can demo the happy path.
findings.context: Exception handling and failure behaviour are the deciding capabilities to test; happy-path demos are not sufficient. — Prospect lists specific failure scenarios to test.

findings.speaker: Tom Alvarez
findings.quote: Can the queue be owned by a team? Not a named person. People change roles constantly here and individual ownership is genuinely one of the reasons our current stuff breaks.
findings.context: Queue/exception ownership must be assignable to a team, not a named person, because individual ownership causes current breakage. — Tom ties this to role churn and current failures.

findings.speaker: Tom Alvarez
findings.quote: We've had integrations die because someone renamed a field or added a picklist value, and the automation just — didn't say anything.
findings.context: Schema-change and mapping-error detection is a requirement; silent integration failures are a past problem. — Prior integrations broke silently after field renames.

findings.speaker: Rachel Morgan
findings.quote: The system of record. If that connector's unreliable, none of the rest matters. After that it's the collaboration and data systems
findings.context: Salesforce connector reliability is the deal-breaker; collaboration and data systems (Slack, Snowflake) next. — Prospect ranks integrations by importance.

findings.speaker: Jon Bell
findings.quote: For your stack it's a mix of native connectors and API-based options. What I'd want to do in a pilot is validate each required operation
findings.context: Vendor says it validates required integration operations in a pilot rather than relying on logos; Salesforce, Slack, Snowflake connectivity is native or API-based. — Vendor claim, not yet validated.

findings.speaker: Tom Alvarez
findings.quote: That matters to me a lot more than a nice dashboard.
findings.context: Auditability and external monitoring of workflow runs (metrics/events exported to own monitoring, audit export) matter more than dashboards. — Tom ranks this above a dashboard.

findings.speaker: Jon Bell
findings.quote: SAML SSO and SCIM on Enterprise.
findings.context: Security baseline required: SOC 2 Type II, SSO, audit logs; SAML SSO and SCIM are Enterprise-only per vendor. — Security is not a gate per Rachel; SSO is a standard requirement.

findings.speaker: Rachel Morgan
findings.quote: That last one needs to be in writing. Not in a demo.
findings.context: Prospect requires that customer workflow data is not used to train a shared model and wants AI disable-able per workspace; AI is secondary. — AI/governance concern; wants it in writing.

findings.speaker: Rachel Morgan
findings.quote: if someone changes a condition on a Friday afternoon and it breaks, can we see exactly what changed?
findings.context: Version history and change control of workflows is a requirement. — Concern about Friday changes breaking flows.

findings.speaker: Elliot Greene
findings.quote: The BAA is the gate. If you can't offer one, we cannot use OrbitFlow for any workflow that may involve protected health information.
findings.context: Security/compliance review is the gate: a BAA is required before OrbitFlow can be used for any workflow that may involve PHI; without it, nothing else proceeds. — Prospect's stated deal-breaker; vendor declined to give a yes on the call and promised a written position in a week.

findings.speaker: Elliot Greene
findings.quote: we need to resolve the BAA question, review your subprocessors, SSO and SCIM, understand retention, and confirm how US data is handled.
findings.context: Prospect's security list included SSO and SCIM provisioning, subprocessor review, retention controls, and US data handling; vendor said SAML SSO and SCIM are on Enterprise. — Security checklist raised before any demo; vendor confirmed baseline capabilities.

findings.speaker: Jon Bell
findings.quote: SAML SSO and SCIM provisioning, both on Enterprise.
findings.context: Vendor stated SAML SSO and SCIM provisioning are available only on the Enterprise package. — Vendor capability claim on baseline certifications.

findings.speaker: Elliot Greene
findings.quote: What happens to data sent to an LLM provider?
findings.context: Prospect's top concern is AI/LLM data handling; they accept AI being excluded from phase one and reviewed separately so automation can proceed. — Security concern about data sent to LLM providers; prospect called it the one they care about most.

findings.speaker: Jon Bell
findings.quote: We also don't use customer workflow content to train a shared OrbitFlow model.
findings.context: Prospect wants the vendor's commitment not to train shared models on customer workflow content to be in the contract, not just marketing. — Vendor claim about training; prospect requires contractual language.

findings.speaker: Elliot Greene
findings.quote: If it only lives in your console it's not an audit trail, it's a screenshot.
findings.context: Prospect requires audit logs to be exportable to their own SIEM; an audit trail living only in the vendor console is not acceptable. — Audit/compliance requirement raised during security discussion.

findings.speaker: Elliot Greene
findings.quote: We have workflows where an admin should know a step failed without seeing the record contents.
findings.context: Field-level masking of run data is required so admins can see a step failed without seeing record contents; vendor says it is designable, not a checkbox. — Run-data visibility requirement; vendor hedged.

findings.speaker: Priya Shah
findings.quote: We're much worse at answering why it was late, or which dependency failed, or whether the same failure happened fifteen times last month.
findings.context: Prospect's core operational requirement is observable run history and telemetry: they can see outcomes but cannot diagnose why workflows were late or which dependency failed. — Current-state pain; prospect values run history over connector count.

findings.speaker: Jon Bell
findings.quote: Open a run and you get every step, inputs, outputs, timing, retries, any human approval.
findings.context: Vendor's run history shows each step, inputs, outputs, timing, retries, and failure routing to exception queues. — Vendor demo of run history feature.

findings.speaker: Elliot Greene
findings.quote: individual ownership is one of the main reasons our current automations rot.
findings.context: Prospect requires exception and queue ownership by teams rather than named individuals, since individual ownership causes automations to rot. — Ownership requirement tied to role churn in current Power Automate flows.

findings.speaker: Priya Shah
findings.quote: That's — okay, that's actually the interesting bit for me. That's the backlog answer, potentially.
findings.context: Prospect wants reusable components so the systems group can build subflows the business assembles, reducing the backlog. — Prospect sees this as the backlog answer; ties to a stated 11-week backlog.

findings.speaker: Priya Shah
findings.quote: A demo with clean data proves nothing.
findings.context: Prospect requires schema-change handling and validation: they have had integrations break silently from renamed fields and want this tested with messy data. — Reliability concern; prospect wants it in the evaluation.

findings.speaker: Priya Shah
findings.quote: The system of record. If that connector's unreliable none of the rest matters.
findings.context: Prospect's must-have integrations are HubSpot, Teams, Jira and Azure AD, with the system-of-record connector as the deal-breaker; Databricks is not phase one. — Integration priorities; vendor said connectors must be validated per operation, not by logo.

findings.speaker: Jon Bell
findings.quote: that's a real design constraint — you'd want to pass references rather than payloads wherever possible
findings.context: Prospect wants a phase-one workflow that routes HubSpot implementation requests into Jira without copying sensitive notes into other systems; pass references, not payloads. — Proposed phase-one candidate; prospect confirmed it is a good candidate.

findings.speaker: Elliot Greene
findings.quote: In practice it lives or dies on whether the permission model is genuinely least-privilege or just a UI that hides things.
findings.context: Prospect wants a permission model that is genuinely least-privilege for a governed operations builder, and wants it demonstrated. — Second use case; prospect skeptical that the permission model is real.

findings.speaker: Priya Shah
findings.quote: I want to reduce dependency, not eliminate engineers.
findings.context: Prospect is wary of no-code claims; vendor says mapping and branching are visual, transformations use expressions, and Enterprise supports packaged JavaScript and a generic REST action. — Technical depth of builder; prospect wants reduced dependency on engineers, not elimination.

findings.speaker: Jon Bell
findings.quote: Version history and change metadata, yes. Rollback and promotion patterns vary by workflow and package.
findings.context: Prospect wants version history and change metadata to see what changed when a workflow breaks; vendor offered version history and change metadata, with rollback varying by package. — Change-management requirement.

findings.speaker: Elliot Greene
findings.quote: Logical is probably enough if the access controls are real and the audit trail crosses both.
findings.context: Prospect wants logical environment separation between sandbox and production with audit trail crossing both. — Environment separation requirement.

findings.speaker: Elliot Greene
findings.quote: EU. We're a US operation with a UK subsidiary. What's the default region?
findings.context: Prospect's data residency concern: US operation with UK subsidiary; vendor would not confirm default region on the call. — Data residency question; vendor deferred to written answer.

findings.speaker: Sophie Reed
findings.quote: Can I set an alert on a failure rate rather than an individual failure? Because sixty automations, if I get an email per failure I'll just filter them into a folder and never look at it.
findings.context: Prospect values monitoring/alerting on failure rates rather than per-failure notifications, to avoid alert fatigue across ~60 automations. — Customer-stated priority on monitoring; Sophie explains why per-failure alerts would be ignored.

findings.speaker: Marcus Lee
findings.quote: When a customer complains.
findings.context: Prospect's core pain is detection of broken automations; failures are currently discovered only when customers complain, and run history visibility is sought. — Marcus describes the current detection mechanism; vendor demoed run history.

findings.speaker: Sophie Reed
findings.quote: That is the most compelling thing you've said.
findings.context: Prospect views reusable templates/subflows as the capability that best addresses their maintenance problem across many automations. — Sophie says the templates speak to the actual problem; vendor pitched consolidating ~60 Zaps into fewer subflows.

findings.speaker: Sophie Reed
findings.quote: A native Shopify trigger is — that's important. If that's a polling hack I'm not interested.
findings.context: Native, event-driven Shopify trigger is a must-have; a polling-based integration would not interest the prospect. Vendor could not confirm trigger coverage and deferred to a written answer. — Shopify is the most critical integration; vendor was unsure and promised written follow-up.

findings.speaker: Sophie Reed
findings.quote: Owned by who?
findings.context: Prospect requires an error-proof exception path when order data is incomplete, with ownership by a team rather than an individual. — Sophie probed handling of incomplete order data during the workflow demo.

findings.speaker: Sophie Reed
findings.quote: What about visibility of who owns what? Because the dead-employee problem is real.
findings.context: Prospect wants visibility into workflow ownership and change, given departed owners; vendor offered version history and dev/production publish controls. — Linked to dead-employee ownership problem.

findings.speaker: Sophie Reed
findings.quote: SSO would be nice rather than mandatory
findings.context: Prospect wants SSO as a nice-to-have rather than mandatory, plus a standard DPA and clarity on UK/EU data processing location (EU residency stated as Enterprise-only). — Security requirements raised during demo; vendor confirmed EU residency only on Enterprise.

findings.speaker: Marcus Lee
findings.quote: With links. Because I don't trust a summary I can't verify.
findings.context: Prospect is interested in the AI-optional steps for a weekly support-theme digest with verifiable source links, and wants usage-based cost modeled. — Marcus has wanted this for two years; he does not trust unverifiable summaries.

findings.speaker: Anika Bose
findings.quote: SAML, SCIM, audit logs, IP restrictions, role separation, private connectivity options, disaster recovery documentation, penetration test material, and German or EU data residency.
findings.context: Customer requires SAML SSO and SCIM provisioning as governance items; vendor says both are supported on Enterprise. — Headline governance requirement from the customer's IT governance lead; vendor stated support in response.

findings.speaker: Jon Bell
findings.quote: SAML SSO and SCIM provisioning — both supported, both on Enterprise.
findings.context: Vendor states SAML SSO and SCIM provisioning are supported and available on the Enterprise package. — Vendor capability claim made in response to the governance list.

findings.speaker: Anika Bose
findings.quote: can audit data be exported to our own systems? We do not accept a vendor console as an audit trail.
findings.context: Customer requires audit logs that can be exported to its own systems; it does not accept a vendor console as the audit trail. — Governance requirement; vendor said audit export is available on Enterprise.

findings.speaker: Jon Bell
findings.quote: Run events and metrics through APIs and webhooks, and audit export on Enterprise.
findings.context: Vendor says run events and metrics can be exported via APIs and webhooks, plus audit export on Enterprise. — Vendor capability claim answering the audit export requirement.

findings.speaker: Martin Vogel
findings.quote: If your platform must call them over the internet, that is not possible for those systems.
findings.context: Customer requires workflows to reach on-premise systems that cannot be exposed to the public internet; private connectivity is a deal-level requirement. Vendor proposed an agent or controlled gateway pattern inside the network, to be validated. — Deployment architecture concern; customer says it is the deciding factor.

findings.speaker: Martin Vogel
findings.quote: the biggest issue is whether SAP and our on-premise systems make the implementation too heavy for the first use case. Everything else is manageable.
findings.context: Customer names SAP S/4HANA connectivity and on-premise SQL Server connectivity as the decisive capability for the first use case; the vendor has not yet shown a viable SAP route. — Customer states this is the crux of whether the deal proceeds; vendor offered API, REST, and agent/gateway options without a one-click SAP connector.

findings.speaker: Jon Bell
findings.quote: What I will not do is tell you there's a one-click SAP connector that solves your estate
findings.context: Vendor declines to claim a one-click SAP connector; offers API-based options, generic REST action, and agent/gateway pattern for on-premise. — Vendor capability statement on SAP integration, explicitly hedged.

findings.speaker: Anika Bose
findings.quote: If business operations own workflows, business operations must not own credentials.
findings.context: Customer requires credentials to be centrally managed so business operations builders never see secrets; secrets must not appear in logs. — Security requirement; vendor said connections are centrally managed and secret values are not displayed in run logs.

findings.speaker: Martin Vogel
findings.quote: That is not negotiable. We do not put anything into production that has not been through test
findings.context: Customer requires separate dev, test and production workspaces with change control, and a second approver; vendor says workspace separation is supported with version history, with rollback/promotion gaps to be mapped. — Deal-level non-negotiable on environment separation.

findings.speaker: Anika Bose
findings.quote: Can the exception queue be owned by a team rather than a named individual?
findings.context: Customer requires exception queues owned by teams rather than individuals, and field-level masking of payloads; vendor said masking is a design conversation, not a checkbox. — Governance and visibility requirement; customer notes individual ownership causes automations to decay.

findings.speaker: Anika Bose
findings.quote: That last point needs to be contractual.
findings.context: Customer requires AI features to be disableable and contractually guaranteed not to train on customer workflow content; vendor says Enterprise can disable AI and does not train shared models on customer content. — Customer excludes generative AI from phase one; vendor states controls.

findings.speaker: Anika Bose
findings.quote: If the system reports that Herr Müller took four days, and that report goes to his manager, that is a different thing.
findings.context: Customer wants individual-level visibility of workflow timing avoided; aggregate at team/queue level to avoid works council co-determination issues. Vendor proposed permissions and reporting design. — Works council (Betriebsrat) requirement tied to monitoring features; a six-month risk.

findings.speaker: Martin Vogel
findings.quote: It is not a tool that business operations should be using directly, and I would not want it to become one.
findings.context: Customer positions the product as a business-owned workflow layer above MuleSoft, not a replacement; customer sees MuleSoft as the integration backbone to keep. — Positioning requirement on how the tool coexists with existing integration platform.

findings.speaker: Anika Bose
findings.quote: Disaster recovery documentation and pen test material — you have these?
findings.context: Customer wants the security and governance pack, including SOC 2, DR and pen test documentation; vendor said these are available. — Governance requirement and vendor commitment.

findings.speaker: Jon Bell
findings.quote: EU data residency is available on Enterprise.
findings.context: Customer requires EU data residency for data; the vendor says EU residency is available on Enterprise but no German region exists. — Data residency requirement; customer says EU may suffice pending legal review.

findings.speaker: Martin Vogel
findings.quote: We can tell you something was late. We are much worse at telling you why, or which dependency failed
findings.context: Vendor states the platform records and visualises run history, letting admins see inputs, steps and failure points; the customer lacks operational telemetry on why processes stall. — Customer pain point on observability that the platform addresses.

findings.speaker: Hannah Cole
findings.quote: The main gates are model-risk and auditability. If you can't satisfy those, connector breadth will not save the project.
findings.context: Prospect states model-risk and auditability are the gating requirements; connector breadth will not save the project if these are not satisfied. — Hannah Cole, Senior Risk Engineer, on what could kill the deal; she treats these as deal-breakers.

findings.speaker: Hannah Cole
findings.quote: The list is: SOC 2, SSO and SCIM, exportable audit history, retention controls, encryption details, subprocessor review, EU residency for European records, and contractual language that our data is not used to train shared AI models.
findings.context: Prospect's audit requirement list includes SOC 2, SSO and SCIM, exportable audit history, retention controls, encryption, subprocessor review, EU residency, and contractual no-training language. — Security/compliance checklist Hannah requires before she will approve.

findings.speaker: Nina Patel
findings.quote: SAML SSO and SCIM on Enterprise.
findings.context: Vendor states SAML SSO and SCIM are available only on the Enterprise package, and audit export is Enterprise-only. — Vendor answer to the security checklist; relevant to SSO as a requirement.

findings.speaker: Hannah Cole
findings.quote: On exportable audit history — define exportable. Because I've had vendors mean "you can download a CSV from a UI" and that is not exportable.
findings.context: Prospect requires exportable, programmatic audit history (API/webhook into their SIEM), not a UI CSV download; this is a key differentiator against Tray. — Hannah pressed for a definition of 'exportable' and said programmatic export is what would decide the choice.

findings.speaker: Hannah Cole
findings.quote: Debugging and audit trail. If your run history is genuinely better to work with, and the audit export is genuinely programmatic, that's the difference. Connector breadth is a tie.
findings.context: Prospect says the deciding factors versus Tray are debugging experience and a genuinely programmatic audit export. — Asked what must be true to choose OrbitFlow over Tray.

findings.speaker: Noah Williams
findings.quote: It's searchable. It's not auditable. Those are different things
findings.context: Prospect needs complete, auditable run history with a record of human approvals and original vs. modified values; the 'not evidenced' audit finding is what started the project. — Auditor previously found exception handling 'not evidenced'; Slack and scripts are searchable but not auditable.

findings.speaker: Hannah Cole
findings.quote: It's the debugging loop and it's error handling. Retry semantics were opaque. We couldn't always tell whether something had run twice.
findings.context: Prospect's top operational pain is weak debugging and retry visibility in large visual workflows; idempotency/retry semantics were opaque in the Tray PoC. — Feedback from the Tray proof of concept.

findings.speaker: Hannah Cole
findings.quote: Add the note about AI outputs not being enforceable as leaf nodes. I want that written down as a known limitation
findings.context: Prospect requires that AI output not be able to feed automated decisions, and flags that OrbitFlow cannot currently enforce this as a hard constraint; it must be recorded as a known limitation. — Model-risk gate; vendor admitted it is a design convention plus review, not a platform switch.

findings.speaker: Noah Williams
findings.quote: Salesforce, Snowflake, Slack, Okta, Jira, and an internal event bus. Required: all of those, plus webhooks and a generic REST connector.
findings.context: Prospect requires an event bus (Kafka-based internal system, not externally reachable) to be integrated, along with Salesforce, Snowflake, Slack, Okta, Jira, webhooks and generic REST. — Integration requirements; vendor flagged the event bus as the architecture question.

findings.speaker: Hannah Cole
findings.quote: We've had integrations fail because someone renamed a field and nothing surfaced.
findings.context: Prospect requires schema-change detection and bad-data testing for integrations after a field rename went unnoticed. — Past integration failure drives the requirement.

findings.speaker: Hannah Cole
findings.quote: Build it, change it, break it, roll it back. Not just build it.
findings.context: Prospect requires a change-management evaluation (dev/prod separation, versioning, rollback) and team-owned exception queues with on-call fallback. — Environment and ownership requirements raised late in the call.

findings.speaker: Noah Williams
findings.quote: If the bill becomes unpredictable as volumes grow, finance will dislike it even if the base price is fine.
findings.context: Prospect wants predictable usage pricing and a capped overage structure, as second-year invoices are a concern. — Commercial concern from Noah, based on past vendor experience.

findings.speaker: Imogen Price
findings.quote: reporting data gets manually copied between HubSpot and spreadsheets
findings.context: Prospect's core pain is manual copying of reporting data between HubSpot and spreadsheets, which they want automated. — Pain point stated early in discovery; drives the need for integration/automation capability.

findings.speaker: Imogen Price
findings.quote: HubSpot, Slack, Google Workspace, Asana, Google Sheets. That's basically it.
findings.context: Prospect's required stack is HubSpot, Slack, Google Workspace, Asana, and Google Sheets; they need native connectors for these. — Listed as the full tool stack; vendor confirmed native connectors.

findings.speaker: Imogen Price
findings.quote: Deal closes in HubSpot, we create the right Asana project from a template, assign the owners, spin up a Slack channel, chase whatever client information's missing, and alert me when a launch date slips.
findings.context: Prospect's required workflow: on HubSpot deal close, create Asana project from template, assign owners, spin up Slack channel, chase missing client info, and alert when launch date slips. — Specific use-case requirement; Imogen repeats it as the use case the recorded demo must show.

findings.speaker: Imogen Price
findings.quote: I see it as useful but too fragile for multi-step onboarding — the minute there's a branch or something needs a person to do something, it falls over.
findings.context: Prospect sees Zapier as too fragile for multi-step onboarding (branches and human steps break it), though it does most of what they need; they have about twenty active Zaps. — Prospect's current tool and its limits; a concern about branching and human-in-loop capability.

findings.speaker: Ben Foster
findings.quote: And if nobody changes the record but the date just passes?
findings.context: Prospect needs the date-slip alert to work even when no record changes (time-based trigger); vendor was unsure and said it may need two workflows. — Concern raised by Ben about event-driven vs scheduled checking; vendor deferred to an SE.

findings.speaker: Imogen Price
findings.quote: If it tells me four accounts are overdue and actually it's six, that's worse than nothing.
findings.context: Prospect requires accuracy of the AI-generated weekly overdue-accounts summary; a wrong count is worse than nothing. — Concern about AI summary reliability; vendor deflected to 'check the underlying data'.

findings.speaker: Ben Foster
findings.quote: We'd want Google login or SAML, normal GDPR terms
findings.context: Prospect requires SSO via Google login or SAML; vendor said SSO is included on all plans, but the prospect doubts it and asked for confirmation. — Security requirement; prospect says competitors gate SSO to enterprise tiers. Vendor said 'fairly sure' and would confirm.

findings.speaker: Ben Foster
findings.quote: Two other vendors we've spoken to had it as an enterprise-only feature and I'd be surprised if you were different.
findings.context: Vendor stated SSO is included on all plans; prospect questioned this because other vendors gate it to enterprise. — Contradiction between vendor claim and prospect's expectation; vendor later hedged.

findings.speaker: Ben Foster
findings.quote: written reassurance that our client documents aren't used to train models. Some of our clients are quite sensitive about that.
findings.context: Prospect requires written assurance that client documents are not used to train AI models, due to client sensitivity. — Data-privacy requirement; vendor promised a DPA.

findings.speaker: Ben Foster
findings.quote: So if the pitch is "we'll standardise your onboarding", that's going to meet resistance from me.
findings.context: Prospect's onboarding customisation per client-services pod must be supported; they reject a rigid standardised workflow. — Requirement for flexible configuration; vendor claimed full flexibility and that pod customisation is configuration.

findings.speaker: Imogen Price
findings.quote: We don't have a dedicated IT team. At all. An operations manager would administer this.
findings.context: Prospect has no IT team; the product must be no-code enough for an operations manager to administer. — Usability requirement; vendor said it is completely no-code.

findings.speaker: Imogen Price
findings.quote: Not a generic one. Ours.
findings.context: Prospect wants a recorded, use-case-specific demo to share internally; a generic demo is not enough. — Evaluation requirement tied to their own workflow.

findings.speaker: Alastair McCrae
findings.quote: I've got a demo environment that's set up for a different use case, so it wouldn't be exactly that.
findings.context: Vendor could not demonstrate the prospect's use case live; demo environment was set up for a different use case. — Vendor gap on demonstrating the required workflow.

findings.speaker: Imogen Price
findings.quote: We're an agency, Alastair. Nobody's auditing our onboarding process.
findings.context: Prospect's must-have is a capability to compare-check accuracy and reliability of automation; prospect is not interested in governance/audit features, seeing them as irrelevant to an agency. — Vendor pitched governance and audit trail as differentiators; prospect rejected the relevance.

findings.speaker: Carlos Mendes
findings.quote: The first-class Dynamics gap is the biggest issue for us.
findings.context: The prospect's most important requirement is a first-class Dynamics integration; the vendor's lack of a deepest first-class Dynamics connector is the biggest issue for them, since Power Automate is already embedded. — Customer states this as the decisive issue; vendor admits the gap. Dynamics 365 and Teams are mandatory.

findings.speaker: Jon Bell
findings.quote: Dynamics 365 and Teams you've said are mandatory.
findings.context: Dynamics 365 and Teams are mandatory for the prospect (as stated by vendor summarizing the requirement). — Vendor's restatement of the customer's requirement; customer did not dispute it.

findings.speaker: Carlos Mendes
findings.quote: Correct. And this is the thing that kills most vendors.
findings.context: Offline tolerance is a hard design constraint: field connectivity is intermittent, so workflows cannot assume the mobile app is online, and the prospect wants the 'not hearing' case handled as an event. — Raised by vendor from notes; customer confirmed and described poor coverage at Scottish and Welsh sites.

findings.speaker: Lucy Hart
findings.quote: We definitely haven't built that.
findings.context: Workflows must handle the absence of a device signal (timeout rule raising an exception); the prospect had not built this before. — Vendor proposed the pattern; customer acknowledged it was missing from their current build.

findings.speaker: Lucy Hart
findings.quote: If a regional supervisor can look at a failed thing and understand what happened without raising a ticket to Carlos's team, that's material.
findings.context: Troubleshooting ease is a key differentiator the prospect needs: supervisors should understand failures without raising tickets to central ops, since complex Power Automate flows are hard to debug. — Pain with incumbent Power Automate; operations team of six supports 2,500 people.

findings.speaker: Carlos Mendes
findings.quote: if we build the remediation pattern once and use it in eight regions, rather than eight regions each building their own.
findings.context: Reusability of remediation patterns across regions is a key requirement the prospect wants proven (build once, use in eight regions). — Vendor agreed to test it rather than claim it.

findings.speaker: Lucy Hart
findings.quote: We're not regulated in that way. It's more that our procurement people prefer it.
findings.context: Security requirements: Azure AD SSO, audit logs, preferably UK data residency, and region-limited access controls. Preference, not regulatory mandate. — Vendor says SAML SSO/SCIM on Enterprise works with Azure AD; UK residency unconfirmed.

findings.speaker: Carlos Mendes
findings.quote: That's — yeah. That's it. The last part especially.
findings.context: Automation requirement centers on the candidate workflow: blocked-installation remediation task creation, regional notification, and keeping Dynamics current as state changes; this is the part the prospect found most compelling. — Prospect's reaction to vendor's candidate workflow.

findings.speaker: Eleanor Brooks
findings.quote: Conflicts is not negotiable. If a workflow makes a conflicts decision, we're finished.
findings.context: Prospect treats conflicts decisions as untouchable; workflow must not have any write path to the conflicts system, enforced at the credential/permission level, not just by design intent. — Security constraint stated as a deal-breaker-level requirement by the prospect's information security manager; vendor responded with read-only connection scoping as the control.

findings.speaker: Samir Khan
findings.quote: Can I audit that? Can I see which connections a workflow uses?
findings.context: Prospect requires auditability of which connections a workflow uses and wants connection scope review as a standing control. — Security review requirement; vendor agreed connection scopes are auditable.

findings.speaker: Nina Patel
findings.quote: We do not have a native concept of a matter-level ethical wall that reads your barrier definitions from iManage and enforces them dynamically. That does not exist.
findings.context: Prospect requires matter-level ethical information barriers enforced by the system. Phase one scoped to barrier-free matters.

findings.speaker: Nina Patel
findings.quote: I'm not going to tell you there's a checkbox.
findings.context: Prospect requires that run data not expose sensitive matter payloads; vendor said field-level masking is a design conversation, not a checkbox, and recommended passing references rather than payloads. — Data-handling concern about run history visibility; vendor said encryption alone does not address who can read the data.

findings.speaker: Samir Khan
findings.quote: Your console is not an audit trail as far as I'm concerned.
findings.context: Prospect requires SIEM-grade audit export; the console alone is not considered an audit trail. Vendor said audit export is on Enterprise and events can be forwarded via APIs/webhooks. — Security/compliance requirement for audit logs.

findings.speaker: Nina Patel
findings.quote: EU data residency is available on Enterprise. UK specifically I need to confirm in writing.
findings.context: Prospect has a hard compliance requirement for UK data residency; vendor offers only EU residency (Enterprise) and could not confirm UK, so it may be a gate. — Public sector clients make the EU/UK distinction material; vendor to confirm in writing within a week.

findings.speaker: Samir Khan
findings.quote: we have a retention policy that says certain operational records are deleted at ninety days, and if your floor is above that, we have a problem.
findings.context: Prospect requires a retention floor at or below their 90-day deletion policy for operational records; vendor must verify the minimum configurable retention. — Compliance requirement; vendor to confirm the actual floor in the pack.

findings.speaker: Samir Khan
findings.quote: Off. For phase one, off.
findings.context: Prospect requires the ability to fully disable AI features for phase one; vendor confirmed Enterprise customers can disable AI and restrict models. — AI is a key security priority; prospect wants it confirmed in writing. Eleanor sees it as phase-one only.

findings.speaker: Samir Khan
findings.quote: our security constraints plus the lack of native legal-system connectors make the integration effort disproportionate.
findings.context: Prospect's main concern is integration effort into iManage and Intapp, which lack native connectors; vendor confirmed only API-based integration via generic REST and webhooks, requiring maintenance. — Key integration requirement and the decisive question for the deal; prospect worries effort is disproportionate to value.

findings.speaker: Eleanor Brooks
findings.quote: It does not have an API.
findings.context: Prospect's stack includes Microsoft 365, Teams, SharePoint, iManage, Intapp, and Azure; a legacy Access database with no API is out of scope for phase one. — Integration requirements; vendor said M365, Teams, SharePoint and Azure are well-supported.

findings.speaker: Eleanor Brooks
findings.quote: Monitoring, mostly. And reusable components.
findings.context: Prospect wants improved monitoring and reusable components beyond their current Power Automate tool, which is used for low-risk admin tasks. — Reason for evaluating OrbitFlow over incumbent.

findings.speaker: Samir Khan
findings.quote: That is genuinely better than what we have.
findings.context: Prospect values full logging of approvals (who approved, when, what changed) and approval forms that collect structured input rather than binary yes/no. — Vendor said run record logs every step and approval identity; prospect said it is better than their email-based status quo.

findings.speaker: Samir Khan
findings.quote: Can workflows call our internal APIs without us exposing them publicly?
findings.context: Prospect requires that workflows can call internal APIs without public exposure and that secrets can be rotated without editing workflows; vendor said secrets rotate at the connection layer. — Technical security requirements; some internal APIs are not publicly reachable.

findings.speaker: Samir Khan
findings.quote: Then that's an argument for restricting who can build AI steps at all.
findings.context: Prospect requires that AI steps be restricted to a separate permission from general workflow building, to prevent privileged content from being passed to a model. — Vendor said it believes this is possible but must confirm.

findings.speaker: Darren Wu
findings.quote: Because it's machine-generated. Nobody has to remember to update it.
findings.context: Darren requires that the data sources driving the flag be machine-generated, since human-maintained fields are unreliable. — Stated data-trust requirement; Snowflake usage is the most trusted source, Salesforce is reliable only for commercial facts, and Zendesk sentiment tagging is not trusted.

findings.speaker: Darren Wu
findings.quote: If Salesforce fields are stale, an elegant workflow will still make bad decisions.
findings.context: Darren's core concern is data quality: stale Salesforce fields would make an automated workflow produce bad decisions. — Raised as the main objection to the proposed cross-system workflow.

findings.speaker: Darren Wu
findings.quote: Looker has the data but no ability to make anything happen.
findings.context: Existing Looker alerts and Gainsight deployment do not produce action; the customer needs a capability that turns signals into actions and joins Zendesk, Snowflake and Salesforce. — Describes the gap in current tooling that the prospect wants filled. findings.speaker: Olivia Grant
findings.quote: The escalation. That's the bit I want.
findings.context: Olivia names the escalation path as the key capability she wants from the workflow. — Prospect's stated priority: an alert without escalation is a notification that gets ignored; the customer's Slack alert channel is already full.

findings.speaker: Darren Wu
findings.quote: I don't want business logic living in two places.
findings.context: Darren says the business logic that defines at-risk accounts should live in one place, owned by the BI team in Snowflake. — Stated after the vendor proposed Snowflake view ownership; the prospect rejects logic split across two systems.

findings.speaker: Darren Wu
findings.quote: SSO, audit logs, retention controls, and a clear boundary around student-level data. That last one is the important one.
findings.context: Darren lists SSO, audit logs, retention controls and a clear boundary around student-level data as security requirements, with student-level data the most important. — Security requirements list; FERPA is the driver for the student-data boundary.

findings.speaker: Darren Wu
findings.quote: Never a student record, never a student identifier.
findings.context: The workflow must operate only on account-level aggregates, with no student records or identifiers. — Stated FERPA constraint. The prospect prefers the restriction be enforced by the data view (impossible rather than forbidden).

findings.speaker: Olivia Grant
findings.quote: That last one matters for us.
findings.context: Olivia says it matters to Inkwell that the vendor does not use customer workflow content to train a shared model. — Responds to the vendor's statement that customer workflow content is not used for training. Relevant to AI-feature requirements.

findings.speaker: Olivia Grant
findings.quote: Because otherwise it's just a plausible paragraph.
findings.context: Olivia wants the weekly AI summary to replace a spreadsheet nobody reads, and it must be trustworthy. — Second requested capability: a weekly narrative summary of customer themes with links back to source tickets and accounts.

findings.speaker: Darren Wu
findings.quote: If there isn't a theme this week, will it invent one?
findings.context: Darren asks that the AI summary abstain when there is no real theme, rather than inventing one. — Requirement for the workflow to refuse low-evidence output; the vendor proposed minimum-evidence thresholds.

findings.speaker: Darren Wu
findings.quote: I'm not having business-critical logic that only exists in a web UI.
findings.context: Darren requires workflow logic to be version-controlled or at least reviewable, and asks whether two versions can be diffed. — Vendor said there is version history and API export but no git integration; a true side-by-side diff was not confirmed.

findings.speaker: Darren Wu
findings.quote: Salesforce fields get overwritten, there's no history on most of them.
findings.context: Darren needs point-in-time historical data to backtest, and notes Salesforce fields are overwritten with no history. — Data limitation affecting the 20-escalation pilot. Snowflake and mostly Zendesk have history; Salesforce does not.

findings.speaker: Olivia Grant

findings.context: Olivia reports that routing escalations to a named CSM breaks constantly because of role changes, so routing to a group is needed. — Vendor proposed routing to a group or dynamic field; the customer confirmed the problem is frequent.

findings.context: Prospect's engineer requires workflow definitions to be reviewable in version control: diffable, with the ability to judge from a PR diff whether a change is safe. — Technical evaluation; the prospect's stated requirement for definition export. findings.speaker: Ava Sinclair
findings.quote: I'm not fine with production connector code and secrets sitting outside engineering review.
findings.context: Prospect requires business-logic authoring by business operations without engineering involvement, with connector code and credential handling under engineering review; this was written down as a requirement. — Core must-have agreed by both prospect sides after a disagreement about governance split.

findings.speaker: Ava Sinclair
findings.quote: Salesforce API limits are the constraint. We've hit them before.
findings.context: Prospect needs Salesforce API rate-limit compatibility and has hit limits before; design must fit a not-generous daily allocation. — Integration constraint on Salesforce, a stated concern.

findings.speaker: Ava Sinclair
findings.quote: I don't care how many logos are on your integrations page. I care about webhooks, REST, and whether the Postgres connector does anything stupid.
findings.context: Prospect values developer-quality APIs (webhooks, REST) and version control over a large connector catalogue. — Vendor recap of prior email; prospect explicitly deprioritises catalogue size.

findings.speaker: Ava Sinclair
findings.quote: Okay. That's a limitation but it's not a blocker.

findings.quote: There should be a linter.

findings.quote: Owning it is forever.
findings.context: Prospect is considering building in-house on Step Functions or Retool Workflows; the build-vs-buy case centres on ongoing maintenance and observability. — Competitive alternative raised by the customer.

draft.answer: Across all 10 prospect calls, the most consistent priorities were security and audit controls (SSO/SCIM, exportable audit logs, no-training AI terms, data residency) [C1], run history and failure visibility [C2], and reliable integrations with the prospect's system of record [C3]. Team-owned exception queues, change control and reusable components also recurred [C4][C5], while some priorities were call-specific [C6].

claims.text: Security and compliance requirements were raised by most prospects. SSO/SCIM was raised by Acme, BrightPath, DeltaWorks, Ember and Juniper, with Cedar & Finch calling SSO nice-to-have and Fable Media wanting Google login or SAML. Prospects named exportable audit logs into their own systems (BrightPath, DeltaWorks, Ember, Harbor Legal) and contractual or written no-training AI terms (Acme, BrightPath, DeltaWorks, Ember, Fable Media, Inkwell). EU or UK data residency came up at BrightPath, DeltaWorks, Ember, Harbor Legal and Juniper. BrightPath called the BAA the gate, and Ember named model-risk and auditability as gates. The vendor said SAML SSO/SCIM and audit export are Enterprise-only.

Run history, debugging and failure visibility were repeatedly emphasised. Acme, BrightPath and DeltaWorks each said they can see that something was late but not why or which dependency failed. Cedar & Finch learns of failures only when customers complain and wants failure-rate alerts. Ember named debugging and a programmatic audit trail as the deciders against Tray. Greenline wants supervisors to understand failures without raising tickets, and Juniper wants run events via API.

Reliable integrations were a priority, with prospects ranking by system of record rather than connector count. Acme and BrightPath said an unreliable system-of-record connector (Salesforce at Acme) is the deal-breaker. Ember said connector breadth is a tie. Juniper deprioritises logo count in favour of webhooks, REST and a safe Postgres connector. Specific gaps: Greenline's first-class Dynamics connector is its biggest issue; DeltaWorks's SAP/on-premise connectivity is decisive and the vendor offered no one-click SAP connector; Harbor Legal's iManage/Intapp need API-only integration; Cedar & Finch needs a native Shopify trigger, which the vendor could not confirm. Several prospects also want schema-change detection after silent integration failures (Acme, BrightPath, Ember).

Prospects wanted exception and queue ownership assigned to teams rather than named individuals, because role churn breaks current automations. This was raised at Acme, BrightPath, Cedar & Finch, DeltaWorks, Ember and Inkwell (escalation routing to a group).

Change control and reuse were recurring needs. Version history and change visibility were sought at Acme, BrightPath, Ember and Inkwell (diffable logic), and DeltaWorks called separate dev/test/prod environments non-negotiable. Reusable templates or subflows were valued at BrightPath, Cedar & Finch (called most compelling), Greenline and Harbor Legal.

Some priorities were specific to one prospect. Greenline needs offline and no-signal tolerance. Harbor Legal needs a write-proof conflicts system and matter-level ethical walls, which the vendor said do not exist natively. Fable Media wants a no-code, flexible builder and rejected governance and audit as irrelevant to an agency. Inkwell wants escalation and trustworthy AI summaries. Juniper's per-event and subflow billing concerns are cost-driven.

conflicts.description: Most prospects treated audit and governance as gating. Fable Media's COO said nobody audits an agency's onboarding and rejected the vendor's governance pitch.
Vendor reps at other calls said SAML SSO/SCIM are Enterprise-only, but on the Fable Media call the vendor said SSO is on all plans (hedged as 'fairly sure'), and the prospect doubted it.
Ember, Juniper and BrightPath de-emphasised connector count in favour of reliability and debugging, while Fable Media needs native connectors for its named stack.

not_covered: Importance was inferred from stated priority and emphasis, not a ranking by the prospects. Deal outcomes were not provided, so it is unknown which capabilities actually decided deals.
assumptions: Prospect calls only; capabilities include features, integrations, security and compliance.

evidence.speaker: Ava Sinclair
evidence.quote: Holds connections open. Doesn't respect statement timeouts. Runs unbounded queries against production.
evidence.context: Prospect requires Postgres connector that does not hold connections open, respects statement timeouts, and avoids unbounded queries against production. — Explicit deal-breaker-style technical concern about the Postgres connector.

evidence.speaker: Carlos Mendes
evidence.quote: The first-class Dynamics gap is the biggest issue for us.
evidence.context: The prospect's most important requirement is a first-class Dynamics integration; the vendor's lack of a deepest first-class Dynamics connector is the biggest issue for them, since Power Automate is already embedded. — Customer states this as the decisive issue; vendor admits the gap. Dynamics 365 and Teams are mandatory.

evidence.speaker: Martin Vogel
evidence.quote: the biggest issue is whether SAP and our on-premise systems make the implementation too heavy for the first use case. Everything else is manageable.
evidence.context: Customer names SAP S/4HANA connectivity and on-premise SQL Server connectivity as the decisive capability for the first use case; the vendor has not yet shown a viable SAP route. — Customer states this is the crux of whether the deal proceeds; vendor offered API, REST, and agent/gateway options without a one-click SAP connector.

evidence.speaker: Jon Bell
evidence.quote: What I will not do is tell you there's a one-click SAP connector that solves your estate
evidence.context: Vendor declines to claim a one-click SAP connector; offers API-based options, generic REST action, and agent/gateway pattern for on-premise. — Vendor capability statement on SAP integration, explicitly hedged.

evidence.speaker: Samir Khan
evidence.quote: our security constraints plus the lack of native legal-system connectors make the integration effort disproportionate.
evidence.context: Prospect's main concern is integration effort into iManage and Intapp, which lack native connectors; vendor confirmed only API-based integration via generic REST and webhooks, requiring maintenance. — Key integration requirement and the decisive question for the deal; prospect worries effort is disproportionate to value.

evidence.speaker: Sophie Reed
evidence.quote: A native Shopify trigger is — that's important. If that's a polling hack I'm not interested.
evidence.context: Native, event-driven Shopify trigger is a must-have; a polling-based integration would not interest the prospect. Vendor could not confirm trigger coverage and deferred to a written answer. — Shopify is the most critical integration; vendor was unsure and promised written follow-up.

evidence.speaker: Tom Alvarez
evidence.quote: We've had integrations die because someone renamed a field or added a picklist value, and the automation just — didn't say anything.
evidence.context: Schema-change and mapping-error detection is a requirement; silent integration failures are a past problem. — Prior integrations broke silently after field renames.

evidence.speaker: Priya Shah
evidence.quote: A demo with clean data proves nothing.
evidence.context: Prospect requires schema-change handling and validation: they have had integrations break silently from renamed fields and want this tested with messy data. — Reliability concern; prospect wants it in the evaluation.

evidence.speaker: Hannah Cole
evidence.quote: We've had integrations fail because someone renamed a field and nothing surfaced.
evidence.context: Prospect requires schema-change detection and bad-data testing for integrations after a field rename went unnoticed. — Past integration failure drives the requirement.

claims.text: Prospects wanted exception and queue ownership assigned to teams rather than named individuals, because role churn breaks current automations. This was raised at Acme, BrightPath, Cedar & Finch, DeltaWorks, Ember and Inkwell (escalation routing to a group).

evidence.speaker: Tom Alvarez
evidence.quote: Can the queue be owned by a team? Not a named person. People change roles constantly here and individual ownership is genuinely one of the reasons our current stuff breaks.
evidence.context: Queue/exception ownership must be assignable to a team, not a named person, because individual ownership causes current breakage. — Tom ties this to role churn and current failures.

evidence.speaker: Elliot Greene
evidence.quote: individual ownership is one of the main reasons our current automations rot.
evidence.context: Prospect requires exception and queue ownership by teams rather than named individuals, since individual ownership causes automations to rot. — Ownership requirement tied to role churn in current Power Automate flows.

evidence.speaker: Sophie Reed
evidence.quote: Owned by who?
evidence.context: Prospect requires an error-proof exception path when order data is incomplete, with ownership by a team rather than an individual. — Sophie probed handling of incomplete order data during the workflow demo.

evidence.speaker: Anika Bose
evidence.quote: Can the exception queue be owned by a team rather than a named individual?
evidence.context: Customer requires exception queues owned by teams rather than individuals, and field-level masking of payloads; vendor said masking is a design conversation, not a checkbox. — Governance and visibility requirement; customer notes individual ownership causes automations to decay.

evidence.speaker: Hannah Cole
evidence.quote: Build it, change it, break it, roll it back. Not just build it.
evidence.context: Prospect requires a change-management evaluation (dev/prod separation, versioning, rollback) and team-owned exception queues with on-call fallback. — Environment and ownership requirements raised late in the call.

evidence.speaker: Olivia Grant
evidence.quote: That happens constantly.
evidence.context: Olivia reports that routing escalations to a named CSM breaks constantly because of role changes, so routing to a group is needed. — Vendor proposed routing to a group or dynamic field; the customer confirmed the problem is frequent.

claims.text: Change control and reuse were recurring needs. Version history and change visibility were sought at Acme, BrightPath, Ember and Inkwell (diffable logic), and DeltaWorks called separate dev/test/prod environments non-negotiable. Reusable templates or subflows were valued at BrightPath, Cedar & Finch (called most compelling), Greenline and Harbor Legal.

evidence.speaker: Rachel Morgan
evidence.quote: if someone changes a condition on a Friday afternoon and it breaks, can we see exactly what changed?
evidence.context: Version history and change control of workflows is a requirement. — Concern about Friday changes breaking flows.

evidence.speaker: Jon Bell
evidence.quote: Version history and change metadata, yes. Rollback and promotion patterns vary by workflow and package.
evidence.context: Prospect wants version history and change metadata to see what changed when a workflow breaks; vendor offered version history and change metadata, with rollback varying by package. — Change-management requirement.

evidence.speaker: Hannah Cole
evidence.quote: Build it, change it, break it, roll it back. Not just build it.
evidence.context: Prospect requires a change-management evaluation (dev/prod separation, versioning, rollback) and team-owned exception queues with on-call fallback. — Environment and ownership requirements raised late in the call.

evidence.speaker: Darren Wu
evidence.quote: I'm not having business-critical logic that only exists in a web UI.
evidence.context: Darren requires workflow logic to be version-controlled or at least reviewable, and asks whether two versions can be diffed. — Vendor said there is version history and API export but no git integration; a true side-by-side diff was not confirmed.

evidence.speaker: Martin Vogel
evidence.quote: That is not negotiable. We do not put anything into production that has not been through test
evidence.context: Customer requires separate dev, test and production workspaces with change control, and a second approver; vendor says workspace separation is supported with version history, with rollback/promotion gaps to be mapped. — Deal-level non-negotiable on environment separation.

evidence.speaker: Priya Shah
evidence.quote: That's — okay, that's actually the interesting bit for me. That's the backlog answer, potentially.
evidence.context: Prospect wants reusable components so the systems group can build subflows the business assembles, reducing the backlog. — Prospect sees this as the backlog answer; ties to a stated 11-week backlog.

evidence.speaker: Sophie Reed
evidence.quote: That is the most compelling thing you've said.
evidence.context: Prospect views reusable templates/subflows as the capability that best addresses their maintenance problem across many automations. — Sophie says the templates speak to the actual problem; vendor pitched consolidating ~60 Zaps into fewer subflows.

evidence.speaker: Carlos Mendes
evidence.quote: if we build the remediation pattern once and use it in eight regions, rather than eight regions each building their own.
evidence.context: Reusability of remediation patterns across regions is a key requirement the prospect wants proven (build once, use in eight regions). — Vendor agreed to test it rather than claim it.

evidence.speaker: Eleanor Brooks
evidence.quote: Monitoring, mostly. And reusable components.
evidence.context: Prospect wants improved monitoring and reusable components beyond their current Power Automate tool, which is used for low-risk admin tasks. — Reason for evaluating OrbitFlow over incumbent.

claims.text: Some priorities were specific to one prospect. Greenline needs offline and no-signal tolerance. Harbor Legal needs a write-proof conflicts system and matter-level ethical walls, which the vendor said do not exist natively. Fable Media wants a no-code, flexible builder and rejected governance and audit as irrelevant to an agency. Inkwell wants escalation and trustworthy AI summaries. Juniper's per-event and subflow billing concerns are cost-driven.

evidence.speaker: Carlos Mendes
evidence.quote: Correct. And this is the thing that kills most vendors.
evidence.context: Offline tolerance is a hard design constraint: field connectivity is intermittent, so workflows cannot assume the mobile app is online, and the prospect wants the 'not hearing' case handled as an event. — Raised by vendor from notes; customer confirmed and described poor coverage at Scottish and Welsh sites.

evidence.speaker: Eleanor Brooks
evidence.quote: Conflicts is not negotiable. If a workflow makes a conflicts decision, we're finished.
evidence.context: Prospect treats conflicts decisions as untouchable; workflow must not have any write path to the conflicts system, enforced at the credential/permission level, not just by design intent. — Security constraint stated as a deal-breaker-level requirement by the prospect's information security manager; vendor responded with read-only connection scoping as the control.

evidence.speaker: Nina Patel
evidence.quote: We do not have a native concept of a matter-level ethical wall that reads your barrier definitions from iManage and enforces them dynamically. That does not exist.
evidence.context: Prospect requires matter-level ethical information barriers enforced by the system. Vendor stated OrbitFlow does NOT have a native matter-level ethical wall that reads barrier definitions from iManage; this is a real unsolved gap that must be designed around and maintained. — Vendor limitation admitted; barriers change weekly, creating an ongoing maintenance burden. Phase one scoped to barrier-free matters.

evidence.speaker: Imogen Price
evidence.quote: We don't have a dedicated IT team. At all. An operations manager would administer this.
evidence.context: Prospect has no IT team; the product must be no-code enough for an operations manager to administer. — Usability requirement; vendor said it is completely no-code.

evidence.speaker: Ben Foster
evidence.quote: So if the pitch is "we'll standardise your onboarding", that's going to meet resistance from me.
evidence.context: Prospect's onboarding customisation per client-services pod must be supported; they reject a rigid standardised workflow. — Requirement for flexible configuration; vendor claimed full flexibility and that pod customisation is configuration.

evidence.speaker: Imogen Price
evidence.quote: We're an agency, Alastair. Nobody's auditing our onboarding process.
evidence.context: Prospect's must-have is a capability to compare-check accuracy and reliability of automation; prospect is not interested in governance/audit features, seeing them as irrelevant to an agency. — Vendor pitched governance and audit trail as differentiators; prospect rejected the relevance.

evidence.speaker: Olivia Grant
evidence.quote: The escalation. That's the bit I want.
evidence.context: Olivia names the escalation path as the key capability she wants from the workflow. — Prospect's stated priority: an alert without escalation is a notification that gets ignored; the customer's Slack alert channel is already full.

evidence.speaker: Olivia Grant
evidence.quote: Because otherwise it's just a plausible paragraph.
evidence.context: Olivia wants the weekly AI summary to replace a spreadsheet nobody reads, and it must be trustworthy. — Second requested capability: a weekly narrative summary of customer themes with links back to source tickets and accounts.

evidence.speaker: Ava Sinclair
evidence.quote: What I do not want is to pay you per event.
evidence.context: Prospect's top volume concern: cannot pay per raw event; only business-relevant events should trigger workflows, and vendor agreed event filtering should stay in the customer's AWS layer. — Millions of product events per day from Segment; cost-driven architecture requirement.

evidence.speaker: Ava Sinclair
evidence.quote: If it's six, the composition pattern you're recommending is also the expensive pattern, and that's a conflict I'd want surfaced before we commit.
evidence.context: Prospect's key pricing/architecture question: whether subflow invocations count as separate billable runs, which would make the recommended composition pattern expensive. — Vendor could not confirm billing semantics and promised written answer.

conflicts.description: Most prospects treated audit and governance as gating. Fable Media's COO said nobody audits an agency's onboarding and rejected the vendor's governance pitch.
Vendor reps at other calls said SAML SSO/SCIM are Enterprise-only, but on the Fable Media call the vendor said SSO is on all plans (hedged as 'fairly sure'), and the prospect doubted it.
Ember, Juniper and BrightPath de-emphasised connector count in favour of reliability and debugging, while Fable Media needs native connectors for its named stack.

not_covered: Importance was inferred from stated priority and emphasis, not a ranking by the prospects. Deal outcomes were not provided, so it is unknown which capabilities actually decided deals.
assumptions: Question concerns prospect calls only (new business), since prospects are the audience named.
Interpreted 'product capabilities' broadly to include features, integrations, security and compliance needs.
Importance is inferred from how often and how emphatically each capability is raised, so the reader should capture stated priority signals.
Prospect calls only; capabilities include features, integrations, security and compliance.
